section.heading: 14.4. Tangent Planes and Linear Approximations
section.paragraph: One of the most important ideas in single-variable calculus is that as we zoom in toward a point on the graph of a differentiable function, the graph becomes indistinguishable from its tangent line and we can approximate the function by a linear function. (See Section 3.10.) Here we develop similar ideas in three dimensions. As we zoom in toward a point on a surface that is the graph of a differentiable function of two variables, the surface looks more and more like a plane (its tangent plane) and we can approximate the function by a linear function of two variables. We also extend the idea of a differential to functions of two or more variables.
section.heading: Tangent Planes
section.paragraph: Suppose a surface $$S$$ has equation $$z = f{({x,y})}$$ , where $$f$$ has continuous first partial derivatives, and let $$P{({x_{0},y_{0},z_{0}})}$$ be a point on $$S$$ . As in Section 14.3, let $$C_{1}$$ and $$C_{2}$$ be the curves obtained by intersecting the vertical planes $$y = y_{0}$$ and $$x = x_{0}$$ with the surface $$S$$ . Then the point $$P$$ lies on both $$C_{1}$$ and $$C_{2}$$ . Let $$T_{1}$$ and $$T_{2}$$ be the tangent lines to the curves $$C_{1}$$ and $$C_{2}$$ at the point $$P$$ . Then the tangent plane to the surface $$S$$ at the point $$P$$ is defined to be the plane that contains both tangent lines $$T_{1}$$ and $$T_{2}$$ . (See Figure 1.)

section.paragraph: You can verify (see Exercise 54) that its partial derivatives exist at the origin and, in fact, $$f_{x}{({0,0})} = 0$$ and $$f_{y}{({0,0})} = 0$$ , but $$f_{x}$$ and $$f_{y}$$ are not continuous. The linear approximation would be $$f{({x,y})} \approx 0$$ , but $$f{({x,y})} = \frac{1}{2}$$ at all points on the line $$y = x$$ . So a function of two variables can behave badly even though both of its partial derivatives exist. To rule out such behavior, we formulate the idea of a differentiable function of two variables.
Recall that for a function of one variable, $$y = f{(x)}$$ , if $$x$$ changes from $$a$$ to $$a + \Delta x$$ , we defined the increment of $$y$$ as
$$\Delta y = f{({a + \Delta x})} - f{(a)}$$
In Chapter 3 we showed that if $$f$$ is differentiable at $$a$$ , then
$${\Delta y = f^{\prime}{(a)}\Delta x + \varepsilon\Delta x} \text{where} \left. \varepsilon\rightarrow 0{as}\Delta x\rightarrow 0 \right.$$
This is Equation 3.4.6.

Now consider a function of two variables, $$z = f{({x,y})}$$ , and suppose $$x$$ changes from $$a$$ to $$a + \Delta x$$ and $$y$$ changes from $$b$$ to $$b + \Delta y$$ . Then the corresponding increment of $$z$$ is
$$\Delta z = f{({a + \Delta x,b + \Delta y})} - f{({a,b})}$$

Thus the increment $$\Delta z$$ represents the change in the value of $$f$$ when $$({x,y})$$ changes from $$({a,b})$$ to $$({a + \Delta x,b + \Delta y})$$ . By analogy with (5) we define the differentiability of a function of two variables as follows.

note.title: Definition
note.heading: Definition
note.paragraph: If $$z = f{({x,y})}$$ , then $$f$$ is differentiable at $$({a,b})$$ if $$\Delta z$$ can be expressed in the form
$$\Delta z = f_{x}{({a,b})}\Delta x + f_{y}{({a,b})}\Delta y + \varepsilon_{1}\Delta x + \varepsilon_{2}\Delta y$$

where $$\varepsilon_{1}$$ and $$\varepsilon_{2}$$ are functions of $$\Delta x$$ and $$\Delta y$$ such that $$\varepsilon_{1}$$ and $$\left. \varepsilon_{2}\rightarrow 0 \right.$$ as $$\left. {({\Delta x,\Delta y})}\rightarrow{({0,0})} \right.$$ .

section.paragraph: Definition 7 says that a differentiable function is one for which the linear approximation (4) is a good approximation when $$({x,y})$$ is near $$({a,b})$$ . In other words, the tangent plane approximates the graph of $$f$$ well near the point of tangency.
It’s sometimes hard to use Definition 7 directly to check the differentiability of a function, but the next theorem provides a convenient sufficient condition for differentiability.

note.title: Theorem
note.heading: Theorem
note.paragraph: If the partial derivatives $$f_{x}$$ and $$f_{y}$$ exist near $$({a,b})$$ and are continuous at $$({a,b})$$ , then $$f$$ is differentiable at $$({a,b})$$ .

section.paragraph: Theorem 8 is proved in Appendix F.

section.heading: Differentials
section.paragraph: For a differentiable function of one variable, $$y = f{(x)}$$ , we define the differential $$dx$$ to be an independent variable; that is, $$dx$$ can be given the value of any real number. The differential of $$y$$ is then defined as
$$dy = f^{\prime}{(x)}dx$$

(See Section 3.10.) Figure 6 shows the relationship between the increment $$\Delta y$$ and the differential $$dy:\Delta y$$ represents the change in height of the curve $$y = f{(x)}$$ and $$dy$$ represents the change in height of the tangent line when $$x$$ changes by an amount $$dx = \Delta x$$ .

section.paragraph: For a differentiable function of two variables, $$z = f{({x,y})}$$ , we define the differentials $$dx$$ and $$dy$$ to be independent variables; that is, they can be given any values. Then the differential $$dz$$ , also called the total differential, is defined by
$$dz = f_{x}{({x,y})}dx + f_{y}{({x,y})}dy = \frac{\partial z}{\partial x}dx + \frac{\partial z}{\partial y}dy$$
(Compare with Equation 9.) Sometimes the notation $$df$$ is used in place of $$dz$$ .

So, in the notation of differentials, the linear approximation (4) can be written as
$$f{({x,y})} \approx f{({a,b})} + dz$$

example.heading: Example 5
example.paragraph: The base radius and height of a right circular cone are measured as $$10$$ cm and $$25$$ cm, respectively, with a possible error in measurement of as much as $$\varepsilon$$ cm in each.

list.item: (a) Use differentials to estimate the maximum error in the calculated volume of the cone.
(b) What is the estimated maximum error in volume if the radius and height are measured with errors up to $$0.1$$ cm?

(a) The volume $$V$$ of a cone with base radius $$r$$ and height $$h$$ is $$V = \pi r^{2}h \slash 3$$ . So the differential of $$V$$ is $$dV = \frac{\partial V}{\partial r}dr + \frac{\partial V}{\partial h}dh = \frac{2\pi rh}{3}dr + \frac{\pi r^{2}}{3}dh$$ Since each error is at most $$\varepsilon$$ cm, we have $$\left| {\Delta r} \right| \leqslant \varepsilon$$ , $$\left| {\Delta h} \right| \leqslant \varepsilon$$ . To estimate the largest error in the volume, we take the largest error in the measurement of $$r$$ and of $$h$$ . Therefore we take $$\mathit{dr} = \varepsilon$$ and $$\mathit{dh} = \varepsilon$$ along with $$r = 10$$ , $$h = 25$$ . This gives $$\Delta V \approx \mathit{dV} = \frac{500\pi}{3}\varepsilon + \frac{100\pi}{3}\varepsilon = 200\pi\varepsilon$$ Thus the maximum error in the calculated volume is about $$200\pi\varepsilon{cm}^{3}$$ .

(b) If the largest error in each measurement is $$\varepsilon = 0.1{cm}$$ , then $$\mathit{dV} = 200\pi(0.1) \approx 63$$ , so the estimated maximum error in volume is about $$63{cm}^{3}$$ . (Note that since the measured volume of the cone is $$V = \pi{(10)}^{2}(25)/3 \approx 2618$$ , this is a relative error of $$63/2618 \approx 0.024 \text{or} 2.4\%$$ .)

section.heading: Functions of Three or More Variables
section.paragraph: Linear approximations, differentiability, and differentials can be defined in a similar manner for functions of more than two variables. A differentiable function is defined by an expression similar to the one in Definition 7. For such functions the linear approximation is
and the linearization $$L{({x,y,z})}$$ is the right side of this expression.
If $$w = f{({x,y,z})}$$ , then the increment of $$w$$ is
$$\Delta w = f{({x + \Delta x,y + \Delta y,z + \Delta z})} - f{({x,y,z})}$$
The differential $$dw$$ is defined in terms of the differentials $$dx$$ , $$dy$$ , and $$dz$$ of the independent variables by
$$dw = \frac{\partial w}{\partial x}dx + \frac{\partial w}{\partial y}dy + \frac{\partial w}{\partial z}dz$$

example.heading: Example 6
example.paragraph: The dimensions of a rectangular box are measured to be $$75$$ cm, $$60$$ cm, and $$40$$ cm, and each measurement is correct to within $$\varepsilon$$ cm.

list.item: (a) Use differentials to estimate the largest possible error when the volume of the box is calculated from these measurements.
(b) What is the estimated maximum error in the calculated volume if the measured dimensions are correct to within $$0.2$$ cm?

(a) If the dimensions of the box are $$x$$ , $$y$$ , and $$z$$ , then its volume is $$V = xyz$$ and so $$dV = \frac{\partial V}{\partial x}dx + \frac{\partial V}{\partial y}dy + \frac{\partial V}{\partial z}dz = yzdx + xzdy + xydz$$ We are given that $$\left| {\Delta x} \right| \leqslant \varepsilon$$ , $$\left| {\Delta y} \right| \leqslant \varepsilon$$ , and $$\left| {\Delta z} \right| \leqslant \varepsilon$$ . To estimate the largest error in the volume, we therefore use $$dx = \varepsilon$$ , $$dy = \varepsilon$$ , and $$dz = \varepsilon$$ together with $$x = 75$$ , $$y = 60$$ , and $$z = 40$$ : $$\Delta V \approx dV = {(60)}{(40)}\varepsilon + {(75)}{(40)}\varepsilon + {(75)}{(60)}\varepsilon = 9900\varepsilon$$ Thus the maximum error in the calculated volume is about $$9900$$ times larger than the error in each measurement taken.

(b) If the largest error in each measurement is $$\varepsilon = 0.2{cm}$$ , then $$\mathit{dV} = 9900(0.2) = 1980$$ , so an error of only $$0.2$$ cm in measuring each dimension could lead to an error of approximately $$1980{cm}^{3}$$ in the calculated volume. (This may seem like a large error, but you can verify that it’s only about $$1\%$$ of the volume of the box.)

section.heading: Applied Project The Speedo LZR Racer
section.paragraph: Many technological advances have occurred in sports that have contributed to increased athletic performance. One of the best known is the introduction, in 2008, of the Speedo LZR racer. It was claimed that this full-body swimsuit reduced a swimmer’s drag in the water. Figure 1 shows the number of world records broken in men’s and women’s long-course freestyle swimming events from 1990 to 2011.* The dramatic increase in 2008 when the suit was introduced led people to claim that such suits were a form of technological doping. As a result, all full-body suits were banned from competition starting in 2010.
L. Foster et al., “Influence of Full Body Swimsuits on Competitive Performance,” Procedia Engineering 34 (2012): 712–17.

section.paragraph: It might be surprising that a simple reduction in drag could have such a big effect on performance. We can gain some insight into this using a simple mathematical model.*
Adapted from http://plus.maths.org/content/swimming.
The speed $$v$$ of an object being propelled through water is given by
$$v{({P,C})} = \left( \frac{2P}{kC} \right)^{1 \slash 3}$$

where $$P$$ is the power being used to propel the object, $$C$$ is the drag coefficient, and $$k$$ is a positive constant. Athletes can therefore increase their swimming speeds by increasing their power or reducing their drag coefficients. But how effective is each of these?

To compare the effect of increasing power versus reducing drag, we need to somehow compare the two in common units. A frequently used approach is to determine the percentage change in speed that results from a given percentage change in power and in drag.

If we work with percentages as fractions, then when power is changed by a fraction $$x$$ (with $$x$$ corresponding to $$100x$$ percent), $$P$$ changes from $$P$$ to $$P + xP$$ .
